title: How to Use This Section
subtitle: Before the doctrines, the ground rules. How to read fairly, where the lines actually fall, and what I am trying to do here.
triageIntro: Not every disagreement carries the same weight. One of the oldest mistakes a Christian can make is to treat a small thing as though the faith itself hung on it, or to treat a large thing as though it did not matter. So before we look at any single doctrine, learn this one framework. It will do more to keep you steady than almost anything else on this site.

triageLevels.label: First order
triageLevels.headline: Essential to the faith itself.
triageLevels.body: These are the things that make Christianity Christianity. The deity and humanity of Jesus. The Trinity. The bodily resurrection. Salvation by grace through faith. Deny one of these and you are no longer describing the Christian faith but something else wearing its clothes. On these we do not bend, and the church across two thousand years has not bent. When this site says a doctrine is first order, it means the historic creeds already settled it, and the burden falls hard on anyone who wants to move the line.

triageLevels.label: Second order
triageLevels.headline: Divides faithful churches, not the faith.
triageLevels.body: These are the doctrines that separate one denomination from another. How baptism works and who receives it. How a church is governed. How the gifts of the Spirit operate today. The fine machinery of how God saves. Sincere, Bible-loving, Jesus-trusting Christians land in different places here, and they always have. You will not commune at the same table on a Sunday morning over some of these, and that is honest. But you will see one another in heaven. When this site marks a doctrine second order, it means take it seriously, hold a real position, and refuse to unchurch the people who disagree.

triageLevels.label: Third order
triageLevels.headline: Room inside one congregation.
triageLevels.body: These are the matters where two members of the same church, sharing the same pew, can simply disagree. The timing of the end times in its finer detail. The age of the earth. How much wine, if any. Whether the days of Genesis one are calendar days. These are worth studying and worth caring about. They are not worth dividing over. When this site marks a doctrine third order, it means hold your view with a loose hand and keep your brother close.

lensHeading: Where I stand, and why I am telling you
lensFlag: DRAFT FOR JAMES TO CONFIRM. This section states the author's own theological commitments in the first person. James, read it closely and make it yours before it goes live. The point is not the specific positions but the honesty of naming them.
lensBody:
Some writers claim to give you the neutral, balanced, view from nowhere. I do not believe there is such a place to stand. Every person who reads the Bible reads it as someone, from somewhere, shaped by a church and a history and a set of convictions they did not invent. The honest thing is not to pretend I have no lens. The honest thing is to tell you what mine is, so you can read me with your eyes open and weigh what I say accordingly.

So here it is. I am a Baptist pastor. I hold to the authority of Scripture as the final word over my life and my church. I confess the historic creeds without crossing my fingers. On the deep questions of how God saves, I have my own settled convictions, and where a doctrine touches them I will tell you plainly that I am giving you my judgment and not the verdict of heaven.

Here is my promise to you in return. When I lay out the positions on a contested doctrine, I will work to state each one the way its best defenders would state it, in its own voice, at its strongest. If I have done my job, you will not be able to tell which view is mine from the way I describe the others. Only when we reach the part of each doctrine called Weighing It will I step forward and say where I think the evidence falls, and even then I will hold it as a pastor holds a fragile thing, not as a man slamming a gavel.
clearlyHeading: The Bible clearly says versus my tradition reads it this way
clearlyBody:
Learn to hear the difference between two sentences, because the whole temperature of the church depends on it.

The first sentence is the Bible clearly says. The second is my tradition reads it this way. They sound close. They are worlds apart. There are things the Bible clearly says, and on those a Christian can stand without apology. Christ is risen. God is love. We are saved by grace. But a great deal of what divides good Christians is not the plain sense of the text at all. It is the framework we bring to the text, the tradition that taught us how to fit the pieces together, the assumptions we absorbed so young we mistake them for the words on the page.

When someone tells you the Bible clearly says a thing, and faithful believers have read that same passage the opposite way for centuries, you are almost certainly looking at a tradition wearing the costume of plain reading. That does not make the tradition wrong. Traditions carry hard-won wisdom. It only means the honest words are I read it this way, and here is why, rather than a claim to obvious truth that quietly accuses everyone who disagrees of not reading their Bible. Throughout this section I will try to keep those two sentences separate, and to flag the moments where I am leaning on a tradition rather than reciting a plain fact.
humilityHeading: How to change your mind well
humilityBody:
Somewhere in this section you will meet a position you have always been told was wrong, stated so fairly that it troubles you. That is the point. Do not panic, and do not rush.

Changing your mind well is a skill, and the church has rarely taught it. The person who never changes their mind has stopped reading. The person who changes it every week never believed anything to begin with. The middle way is to hold your convictions firmly enough to live by them and loosely enough to be corrected by Scripture, by wiser readers, by the slow work of the Spirit over years. When a new argument lands, sit with it. Pray over it. Take it to people who disagree with you and ask them to make it stronger, not weaker. Be willing to say I was wrong about that, which are four of the most spiritually healthy words a person can learn to say. And be equally willing, after all of it, to stay where you were because the evidence held. Doubt is not the enemy of faith. Lazy certainty is.
formationHeading: This is for your soul, not your scorecard
formationBody:
One last word before you begin. It is possible to learn all of this and become worse. Knowledge puffs up, Paul wrote to a church that prized its cleverness, and he was not being quaint. There is a way of studying theology that turns a person into a collector of arguments, quick to win and slow to love, who can name every heresy and has the patience of none of the saints.

That is not what this is for. The doctrines on this site are not trophies. They are the load-bearing truths your life will lean on when it cracks, and it will crack. You are not here to win arguments at the family table. You are here to know the God who saved you more truly, so that you can love him more deeply and love the people he made more patiently. If your theology is making you harder to live with, you have taken a wrong turn somewhere, and the turn was not in the doctrine. Read slowly. Read prayerfully. Let it land in your knees before it lands in your mouth.
